notes.front: What are the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR)?
notes.back: Parts 171 through 180 of Title 49, chapter I: the federal rules for transporting hazardous materials.
notes.explanation: The definitions section of part 171 gives both the full name and the short form HMR.
notes.example: Like a road traffic code, but for dangerous cargo: it covers how the goods are classed, packed, marked and documented as well as how they move.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “HMR”, p. 29
notes.evidence: HMR means the Hazardous Materials Regulations, parts 171 through 180 of this chapter.

notes.front: Who issues the HMR, and on whose authority?
notes.back: The Administrator of the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), under authority delegated by the Secretary of Transportation.
notes.explanation: The Secretary holds the power under the statute and passed the rule-making job for safe and secure hazmat transport to this Administrator.
notes.example: Like a national aviation authority that writes the rules pilots follow, but for hazardous cargo on every mode of transport.
introduces: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1 (revised as of 1 October 2025), introductory text, p. 1
notes.evidence: the Secretary delegated authority to issue regulations for the safe and secure transportation of hazardous materials in commerce to the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administrator. The Administrator issues the Hazardous Materials Regulations
uses: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration

notes.front: What is “Federal hazardous materials transportation law”?
notes.back: 49 U.S.C. 5101 et seq.: the statute that directs the Secretary of Transportation to regulate hazmat transport in commerce.
notes.explanation: The HMR are the regulations made under this statute; the statute sets the aim of safe and secure transportation.
notes.example: Like an Act of Parliament and the detailed regulations made under it: the statute grants the power, the HMR fill in the detail.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1 (revised as of 1 October 2025), introductory text, p. 1
notes.evidence: Federal hazardous materials transportation law (49 U.S.C. 5101 et seq.) directs the Secretary of Transportation to establish regulations for the safe and secure transportation of hazardous materials in commerce

notes.front: What is a hazardous material (hazmat) under the HMR?
notes.back: A substance or material the Secretary of Transportation has found able to pose an unreasonable risk to health, safety and property in commerce, and designated.
notes.explanation: The designation is made under section 5103 of Federal hazardous materials transportation law (49 U.S.C. 5103).
notes.example: Like a controlled drug, the label comes from an official designation, but here the list covers things such as fuels, gases and corrosive liquids moved in commerce.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous material”, p. 27
notes.evidence: Hazardous material means a substance or material that the Secretary of Transportation has determined is capable of posing an unreasonable risk to health, safety, and property when transported in commerce, and has designated as hazardous under section 5103

notes.front: In the HMR, what is a “person”?
notes.back: An individual, company or other body, including a government or Indian Tribe, that offers or transports hazmat commercially, or makes or tests qualified packagings.
notes.explanation: The list runs from individuals through corporations and partnerships to governments, so the HMR reach public bodies as well as businesses.
notes.example: Like “legal person” in company law, but tied to an activity: the body must be offering, transporting or making packagings for hazmat.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Person”, p. 33
notes.evidence: Person means an individual, corporation, company, association, firm, partnership, society, joint stock company; or a government, Indian Tribe, or authority of a government or Tribe, that offers a hazardous material for transportation in commerce

notes.front: What is a carrier under the HMR?
notes.back: A person who transports passengers or property in commerce by rail car, aircraft, motor vehicle or vessel.
notes.explanation: The definition names four modes of transport, and the carrier is whoever does the moving in commerce by any of them.
notes.example: Like a haulier or an airline that moves goods for customers, rather than the company that made or packed them.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Carrier”, p. 24
notes.evidence: Carrier means a person who transports passengers or property in commerce by rail car, aircraft, motor vehicle, or vessel.

notes.front: Who is a hazmat employee?
notes.back: A person employed full-time, part-time or temporarily by a hazmat employer who, in that work, directly affects hazardous materials transportation safety.
notes.explanation: The test is the effect on transport safety, and it covers temporary and part-time staff as well as full-time staff.
notes.example: Like a “designated person” in a safety scheme: a dispatcher who fills in the dangerous goods paperwork counts, whatever their job title.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Employed on a full-time, part time, or temporary basis by a hazmat employer and who in the course of such full time, part time or temporary employment directly affects hazardous materials transportation safety

notes.front: Who is a hazmat employer?
notes.back: A person who employs or uses at least one hazmat employee and transports hazmat in commerce or causes it to be transported, among other activities.
notes.explanation: The first limb of the definition joins two tests: having at least one hazmat employee, and taking part in hazmat transport.
notes.example: Like a firm with one driver who delivers cylinders of welding gas: one hazmat employee is enough.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employer”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Hazmat employer means: (1) A person who employs or uses at least one hazmat employee on a fulltime, part time, or temporary basis; and who: (i) Transports hazardous materials in commerce; (ii) Causes hazardous materials to be transported in commerce

notes.front: What is a pre-transportation function?
notes.back: A function specified in the HMR that is required to assure safe transportation of a hazardous material in commerce, such as determining its hazard class.
notes.explanation: The definition gives a list that begins with determining the hazard class, and 171.1(b) repeats the list of these functions.
notes.example: Like preparing a parcel at the post office counter before it is collected, but for hazmat: classifying, packing and marking it.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Pre-transportation function”, p. 33
notes.evidence: Pre-transportation function means a function specified in the HMR that is required to assure the safe transportation of a hazardous material in commerce, including— (1) Determining the hazard class of a hazardous material.

notes.front: What is storage incidental to movement?
notes.back: Storage of a transport vehicle, freight container or package holding hazmat, by any person, between the carrier taking possession and delivery to the destination shown.
notes.explanation: It sits inside the period of transportation, so it is one of the transportation functions under 171.1(c).
notes.example: Like a parcel waiting overnight in a courier’s depot on its way to you, but holding hazmat.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(4) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: Storage of a transport vehicle, freight container, or package containing a hazardous material by any person between the time that a carrier takes physical possession of the hazardous material for the purpose of transporting it until the package containing the hazardous material has been delivered to the destination

notes.front: What is a packaging?
notes.back: A receptacle and any other components or materials needed for it to perform its containment function under the minimum packing requirements.
notes.explanation: The definition is about the empty means of containment; radioactive materials packaging has its own definition in 173.403.
notes.example: Like an empty steel drum with its lid and gasket, before anything is put in it.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Packaging”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Packaging means a receptacle and any other components or materials necessary for the receptacle to perform its containment function in conformance with the minimum packing requirements of this subchapter.

notes.front: What is a package (or outside package)?
notes.back: A packaging plus its contents.
notes.explanation: A package is what exists once a packaging has been filled; for radioactive materials, 173.403 has its own definition.
notes.example: Like the difference between an empty bottle and a bottle of wine: the wine bottle is the package.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Package or Outside Package”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Package or Outside Package means a packaging plus its contents. For radioactive materials, see § 173.403 of this subchapter.

notes.front: What is a bulk packaging?
notes.back: A packaging, other than a vessel or barge, in which hazmat is loaded with no intermediate containment, including a transport vehicle or freight container.
notes.explanation: The definition turns on how the material sits in the packaging, not on the packaging’s name.
notes.example: Like a road tanker of fuel, where the liquid sits directly in the tank rather than in drums.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Bulk packaging”, p. 23
notes.evidence: Bulk packaging means a packaging, other than a vessel or a barge, including a transport vehicle or freight container, in which hazardous materials are loaded with no intermediate form of containment.

notes.front: What is a non-bulk packaging for a liquid?
notes.back: A packaging with a maximum capacity of 450 L (119 gallons) or less as a receptacle for a liquid.
notes.explanation: The definition sets separate limits for liquids, solids and gases; this is the liquid limit.
notes.example: Like a jerrycan or a standard drum of solvent, well under the 450 L limit.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Non-bulk packaging”, p. 31
notes.evidence: Non-bulk packaging means a packaging which has: (1) A maximum capacity of 450 L (119 gallons) or less as a receptacle for a liquid;

notes.front: What is a transport vehicle?
notes.back: A cargo-carrying vehicle, such as an automobile, van, tractor, truck, semitrailer, tank car or rail car, used to transport cargo by any mode.
notes.explanation: The definition is mode-neutral: road and rail vehicles are both listed.
notes.example: Like a box van making deliveries.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Transport vehicle”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Transport vehicle means a cargo-carrying vehicle such as an automobile, van, tractor, truck, semitrailer, tank car or rail car used for the transportation of cargo by any mode.

notes.front: What is a freight container?
notes.back: A reusable container having a volume of 64 cubic feet or more.
notes.explanation: The rest of the definition, on the next page, adds its design for lifting and its purpose.
notes.example: Like a shipping container lifted from a ship onto a lorry with its cargo still inside.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Freight container”, p. 26
notes.evidence: Freight container means a reusable container having a volume of 64 cubic feet or more, designed and constructed

notes.front: Under the 10-1-25 text, what is a hazardous substance?
notes.back: A material listed in appendix A to 172.101, in one package at or above its reportable quantity, and meeting a concentration test when mixed.
notes.explanation: All the conditions must be met: being listed is not enough without the quantity in one package.
notes.example: Like a customs threshold: the goods are named on a list, but they only count once one package holds enough.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous substance”, p. 27
notes.evidence: Hazardous substance for the purposes of this subchapter, means a material, including its mixtures and solutions, that— (1) Is listed in the appendix A to § 172.101 of this subchapter; (2) Is in a quantity, in one package, which equals or exceeds the reportable quantity (RQ)

notes.front: Under the 10-1-25 text, what is a reportable quantity (RQ)?
notes.back: The quantity given in column 2 of Table 1 or column 3 of Table 2 of appendix A to 172.101 for a listed material.
notes.explanation: It is the threshold that makes a listed material a hazardous substance when one package holds that much or more.
notes.example: Like a weight limit printed next to each item on a list: at or above it, the rules for hazardous substances apply.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Reportable quantity”, p. 35
notes.evidence: Reportable quantity (RQ) for the purposes of this subchapter, means the quantity specified in Column 2 of Table 1 or Column 3 of Table 2 of appendix A to § 172.101 for any material identified in Column 1 of the tables.

notes.front: What is a hazardous waste under the HMR?
notes.back: Any material subject to the Hazardous Waste Manifest Requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, in part 262 of title 40.
notes.explanation: The HMR borrow the environmental agency’s test instead of writing their own.
notes.example: Like spent solvent from a paint shop that must travel with a waste manifest to a treatment plant.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous waste”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Hazardous waste, for the purposes of this chapter, means any material that is subject to the Hazardous Waste Manifest Requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency specified in 40 CFR part 262.

notes.front: What is an elevated temperature material?
notes.back: A material offered or transported in a bulk packaging while hot enough to meet one of three temperature tests in 171.8.
notes.explanation: The definition only applies in a bulk packaging, and each test is a temperature for a liquid or a solid.
notes.example: Like hot liquid carried in an insulated tanker, where the heat itself is part of the hazard.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Elevated temperature material”, p. 26
notes.evidence: Elevated temperature material means a material which, when offered for transportation or transported in a bulk packaging:

notes.front: What is a material poisonous by inhalation (PIH)?
notes.back: A gas or liquid meeting the inhalation toxicity criteria and assigned to a hazard zone, or a material a special provision names an inhalation hazard.
notes.explanation: The same definition also calls it “material toxic by inhalation”, so the two names mean one thing.
notes.example: Like a gas where breathing a small amount is the main danger, rather than fire or burns.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Material poisonous by inhalation”, p. 30
notes.evidence: Material poisonous by inhalation or Material toxic by inhalation means:

notes.front: What is the primary hazard of a material?
notes.back: The hazard class of the material as assigned in the 172.101 table.
notes.explanation: The table fixes it, so the shipper looks it up rather than choosing it.
notes.example: Like the main heading on a warning notice, chosen by the regulator’s table rather than by the shipper.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Primary hazard”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Primary hazard means the hazard class of a material as assigned in the § 172.101 table.

notes.front: What is a subsidiary hazard?
notes.back: A hazard of a material other than its primary hazard.
notes.explanation: The definition points back to primary hazard, so the two are read together.
notes.example: Like a second warning on a product: the main class first, then any other danger it also presents.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Subsidiary hazard”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Subsidiary hazard means a hazard of a material other than the primary hazard. (See primary hazard).

notes.front: What is a residue under the HMR?
notes.back: The hazmat left in a packaging after it has been unloaded as far as practicable, before refilling or cleaning and purging.
notes.explanation: The definition names a tank car as one example of a packaging that can hold a residue.
notes.example: Like the film of paint left in a tin you have emptied but not washed.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Residue”, p. 35
notes.evidence: Residue means the hazardous material remaining in a packaging, including a tank car, after its contents have been unloaded to the maximum extent practicable and before the packaging is either refilled or cleaned of hazardous material and purged to remove any hazardous vapors.

notes.front: What is a special permit?
notes.back: A document issued by the Associate Administrator under 49 U.S.C. 5117 letting a person do something not otherwise permitted by the HMR.
notes.explanation: It is issued under the statute, so it can authorise a function that subchapter A or C would not otherwise allow.
notes.example: Like a planning variance for one site, but for a hazmat function the regulations would otherwise forbid.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Special permit”, p. 36
notes.evidence: Special permit means a document issued by the Associate Administrator, the Associate Administrator’s designee, or as otherwise prescribed in the HMR, under the authority of 49 U.S.C. 5117 permitting a person to perform a function that is not otherwise permitted

notes.front: What is a limited quantity (Ltd Qty)?
notes.back: Where a section for a material says so, the maximum amount of that hazmat for which there is a specific labelling or packaging exception.
notes.explanation: It only exists where a section applicable to the material specifies it, so it is not a general allowance.
notes.example: Like a hand-luggage allowance for liquids: below the set amount, some of the usual rules are relaxed.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Limited quantity”, p. 29
notes.evidence: Limited quantity, when specified as such in a section applicable to a particular material, means the maximum amount of a hazardous material for which there is a specific labeling or packaging exception.

notes.front: What is a technical name?
notes.back: A recognised chemical or microbiological name currently used in scientific and technical handbooks, journals and texts.
notes.explanation: Generic descriptions may be used if they readily identify the general chemical or microbiological group.
notes.example: Like the name a chemist would look up in a reference book, rather than the brand on the tin.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Technical name”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Technical name means a recognized chemical name or microbiological name currently used in scientific and technical handbooks, journals, and texts. Generic descriptions are authorized for use as technical names provided they readily identify the general chemical group, or microbiological group.

notes.front: What is a shipping paper?
notes.back: A shipping order, bill of lading, manifest or other shipping document serving a similar purpose, prepared under subpart C of part 172.
notes.explanation: The name of the document does not matter; what matters is that it serves that purpose and follows subpart C.
notes.example: Like a delivery note that travels with the goods, but with the hazmat description the regulations require.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Shipping paper”, p. 35
notes.evidence: Shipping paper means a shipping order, bill of lading, manifest or other shipping document serving a similar purpose and prepared in accordance with subpart C of part 172 of this chapter.

notes.front: What is a proper shipping name?
notes.back: The name of the hazardous material shown in Roman print (not italics) in the 172.101 table.
notes.explanation: The typeface in the table separates the official name from other words printed beside it.
notes.example: Like the official name on a register, as opposed to a nickname or description written next to it.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Proper shipping name”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Proper shipping name means the name of the hazardous material shown in Roman print (not italics) in § 172.101 of this subchapter.

notes.front: Regulations under Federal hazardous materials transportation law govern safety aspects, {{c1::including security}}, of hazmat transportation.
notes.explanation: Security sits inside the scope of the regulations alongside safety.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1 (revised as of 1 October 2025), introductory text, p. 1
notes.evidence: Regulations prescribed in accordance with Federal hazardous materials transportation law shall govern safety aspects, including security, of the transportation of hazardous materials that the Secretary considers appropriate.

notes.front: A factory makes steel drums and sells them marked as qualified for hazmat. It never fills or ships a drum itself. Do the HMR apply to it?
notes.back: B: Yes, because it manufactures and marks a packaging represented as qualified for hazmat transport.
notes.explanation: 171.1(a) applies the HMR to each person who manufactures or marks a packaging represented as qualified for hazmat transport.
notes.choices:
A) No, because it never offers hazmat for transportation
B) Yes, because it manufactures and marks a packaging represented as qualified for hazmat transport
C) No, because only carriers are subject to the HMR
D) Only if it also fills the drums
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 171.1(a) does not require the maker to offer hazmat. C is wrong: 171.1(a) and (b) reach packaging makers and shippers, not only carriers. D is wrong: manufacturing and marking are enough on their own.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(a) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: Requirements in the HMR apply to each person who manufactures, fabricates, marks, maintains, reconditions, repairs, or tests a packaging or a component of a packaging that is represented, marked, certified, or sold as qualified

notes.front: Under 171.1(b), who must meet the HMR’s pre-transportation requirements?
notes.back: Each person who offers, causes to be transported, or transports hazmat in commerce and performs, or is responsible for performing, a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: Being responsible for the function is enough, as is doing it under contract with a federal body.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: Requirements in the HMR apply to each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation in commerce, causes a hazardous material to be transported in commerce, or transports a hazardous material in commerce and who performs or is responsible for performing a pre-transportation function

notes.front: The fourteen pre-transportation functions listed in 171.1(b) are introduced with the words “include, {{c1::but are not limited to}}”.
notes.explanation: The list is open, so a function missing from it can still be a pre-transportation function.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: Pre-transportation functions include, but are not limited to, the following:

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(1), {{c1::determining the hazard class}} of a hazardous material is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: It is first in the 171.1(b) list, and the 171.8 definition of pre-transportation function gives it as its first example.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (1) Determining the hazard class of a hazardous material.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(2), {{c1::selecting}} a hazardous materials packaging is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: Choosing the packaging is listed separately from filling it, which is 171.1(b)(3).
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (2) Selecting a hazardous materials packaging.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(3), filling a hazardous materials packaging, {{c1::including a bulk packaging}}, is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: The words cover a tank or other bulk packaging as well as drums and boxes.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (3) Filling a hazardous materials packaging, including a bulk packaging.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(4), securing a closure on a filled or partly filled package, or on one containing a {{c1::residue}}, is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: Closing a packaging that holds only a residue still counts, not just a full one.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (4) Securing a closure on a filled or partially filled hazardous materials package or container or on a package or container containing a residue of a hazardous material.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(5), {{c1::marking}} a package to indicate that it contains a hazardous material is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: Marking is listed apart from labelling, which is 171.1(b)(6).
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (5) Marking a package to indicate that it contains a hazardous material.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(6), {{c1::labeling}} a package to indicate that it contains a hazardous material is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: Labelling follows marking in the list; both tell handlers that the package holds hazmat.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (6) Labeling a package to indicate that it contains a hazardous material.

notes.front: An office clerk types up the bill of lading describing a drum of hazmat before collection. Which pre-transportation function is this?
notes.back: Preparing a shipping paper (171.1(b)(7)).
notes.explanation: A bill of lading is one of the documents that can be a shipping paper, and preparing one is on the 171.1(b) list.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b)(7) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (7) Preparing a shipping paper. (8) Providing and maintaining emergency response information.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(8), providing and {{c1::maintaining}} emergency response information is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: The function covers maintaining the information, not only providing it.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (8) Providing and maintaining emergency response information.

notes.front: A supervisor checks a colleague’s finished shipping paper against the HMR before the load leaves. Which pre-transportation function is this?
notes.back: Reviewing a shipping paper to verify compliance with the HMR or international equivalents (171.1(b)(9)).
notes.explanation: Reviewing is listed separately from preparing, so the checker performs a pre-transportation function too.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b)(9) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (9) Reviewing a shipping paper to verify compliance with the HMR or international equivalents.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(10), what pre-transportation function falls on a person importing hazmat into the United States?
notes.back: Giving the shipper timely and complete information on the HMR requirements that will apply to the material’s transport within the United States.
notes.explanation: The duty falls on the importer, and the information concerns the HMR requirements that apply within the United States.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b)(10) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (10) For each person importing a hazardous material into the United States, providing the shipper with timely and complete information as to the HMR requirements that will apply to the transportation of the material within the United States.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(11), {{c1::certifying}} that a hazardous material is in proper condition for transportation under the HMR is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: Certifying is listed as a function in its own right, apart from preparing the shipping paper.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (11) Certifying that a hazardous material is in proper condition for transportation in conformance with the requirements of the HMR.

notes.front: At the shipper’s dock, before any carrier is present, a worker loads drums of hazmat into a trailer and braces them. Which pre-transportation function is this?
notes.back: Loading, blocking and bracing a hazmat package in a freight container or transport vehicle (171.1(b)(12)).
notes.explanation: The same work counts as loading incidental to movement only when carrier personnel do it or are present.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b)(12) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (12) Loading, blocking, and bracing a hazardous materials package in a freight container or transport vehicle.

notes.front: Under 171.1(b)(13), {{c1::segregating}} a hazmat package in a freight container or transport vehicle from incompatible cargo is a pre-transportation function.
notes.explanation: The same segregating counts as loading incidental to movement when carrier personnel do it or are present.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (13) Segregating a hazardous materials package in a freight container or transport vehicle from incompatible cargo.

notes.front: A shipper’s employee fixes placards to a trailer to show it contains hazmat. Which pre-transportation function is this?
notes.back: Selecting, providing or affixing placards for a freight container or transport vehicle (171.1(b)(14)).
notes.explanation: Placards identify the whole vehicle or container, whereas marking and labelling apply to packages.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(b)(14) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: (14) Selecting, providing, or affixing placards for a freight container or transport vehicle to indicate that it contains a hazardous material.

notes.front: How does 171.8 define “transportation or transport”?
notes.back: The movement of property and loading, unloading, or storage incidental to that movement.
notes.explanation: This matches the four transportation functions listed in 171.1(c).
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Transportation or transport”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Transportation or transport means the movement of property and loading, unloading, or storage incidental to that movement.

notes.front: Under 171.1(c), when does transportation of a hazmat in commerce begin?
notes.back: When a carrier takes physical possession of the hazmat for the purpose of transporting it.
notes.explanation: Before that moment the material is still with the offeror, and transportation continues until delivery to the destination shown.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: Transportation of a hazardous material in commerce begins when a carrier takes physical possession of the hazardous material for the purpose of transporting it

notes.front: Under 171.1(c), when does transportation of a hazmat package end?
notes.back: On delivery to the destination shown on a shipping document, package marking or other medium; for a rail car, on reaching private track or siding.
notes.explanation: The destination indicated on the paperwork or marking is the end point, with a separate rule for rail cars.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: continues until the package containing the hazardous material is delivered to the destination indicated on a shipping document, package marking, or other medium, or, in the case of a rail car, until the car is delivered to a private track or siding.

notes.front: A builders’ merchant sends its own driver in its own lorry to take cylinders of gas to a site. When does transportation in commerce begin?
notes.back: B: When the driver takes possession of the cylinders for the purpose of transporting them.
notes.explanation: For a private motor carrier, 171.1(c) starts transportation when the motor vehicle driver takes possession of the hazmat to transport it.
notes.choices:
A) When the cylinders are filled
B) When the driver takes possession of the cylinders for the purpose of transporting them
C) When the lorry joins a public road
D) When the shipping paper is signed
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: filling is a pre-transportation function. D is wrong: certifying is also a pre-transportation function. C is wrong: the rule ties the start to the driver’s possession, not to the road.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 2
notes.evidence: For a private motor carrier, transportation of a hazardous material in commerce begins when a motor vehicle driver takes possession of a hazardous

notes.front: The first transportation function in 171.1(c) is {{c1::movement}} of a hazardous material by rail car, aircraft, motor vehicle or vessel.
notes.explanation: Movement is the core of transportation; the other three functions are loading, unloading and storage incidental to it.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(1) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: (1) Movement. Movement of a hazardous material by rail car, aircraft, motor vehicle, or vessel

notes.front: When is loading packaged hazmat onto a vehicle “loading incidental to movement”?
notes.back: When carrier personnel do the loading, or it is done in their presence, for the purpose of transporting the hazmat.
notes.explanation: It includes blocking, bracing and segregating packages, so the same acts can fall on either side of the line depending on who is present.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(2) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: including blocking and bracing a hazardous materials package in a freight container or transport vehicle, and segregating a hazardous materials package in a freight container or transport vehicle from incompatible cargo, when performed by carrier personnel or in the presence of carrier personnel.

notes.front: For a bulk packaging, what is loading incidental to movement?
notes.back: Filling the packaging with hazmat for transport when carrier personnel perform it or are present, including transloading.
notes.explanation: Filling a bulk packaging is otherwise a pre-transportation function under 171.1(b)(3); the carrier’s presence changes its category.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(2) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: For a bulk packaging, loading incidental to movement is filling the packaging with a hazardous material for the purpose of transporting it when performed by carrier personnel or in the presence of carrier personnel

notes.front: For a private motor carrier, when is unloading hazmat “unloading incidental to movement”?
notes.back: When the driver of the vehicle being unloaded straight after the movement is present during the unloading.
notes.explanation: For other carriers the test is whether carrier personnel perform the unloading or are present.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(3) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: in the case of a private motor carrier, while the driver of the motor vehicle from which the hazardous material is being unloaded immediately after movement is completed is present during the unloading operation.

notes.front: When is storage at a destination shown on a shipping document still storage incidental to movement?
notes.back: When the original shipping documentation identifies the shipment as a through-shipment and names its final destination or destinations.
notes.explanation: Such a stop, for example at a transloading facility, is only a stage on the way to the final destination.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(4)(i) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: Storage at the destination shown on a shipping document, including storage at a transloading facility, provided the original shipping documentation identifies the shipment as a through-shipment and identifies the final destination or destinations of the hazardous material

notes.front: Storage incidental to movement does not include storage of a hazardous material at its {{c1::final destination}} as shown on a shipping document.
notes.explanation: Once the material is stored at its final destination, it has left transportation.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(4)(ii) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: (ii) Storage incidental to movement does not include storage of a hazardous material at its final destination as shown on a shipping document.

notes.front: Drums of hazmat wait three days at a transloading depot. The original shipping documents show a through-shipment to a plant in another state. How do the HMR treat the stay at the depot?
notes.back: B: As storage incidental to movement, subject to the HMR.
notes.explanation: Storage at a transloading facility counts as incidental to movement when the documents identify a through-shipment and its final destination.
notes.choices:
A) As storage after delivery, outside the HMR
B) As storage incidental to movement, subject to the HMR
C) As a pre-transportation function
D) As outside the HMR, because the depot is not the carrier
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the depot is not the final destination shown. C is wrong: storage during transport is a transportation function. D is wrong: storage incidental to movement covers storage “by any person”.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(4)(i) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: including storage at a transloading facility, provided the original shipping documentation identifies the shipment as a through-shipment and identifies the final destination or destinations of the hazardous material

notes.front: Under 171.1(d)(1), what storage at the offeror’s facility is outside the HMR?
notes.back: Storage of a hazmat package, container or vehicle at the offeror facility before a carrier takes possession of it for transport.
notes.explanation: Transportation has not yet begun, because it starts when the carrier takes possession.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(1) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: (1) Storage of a freight container, transport vehicle, or package containing a hazardous material at an offeror facility prior to a carrier taking possession of the hazardous material for movement in transportation in commerce

notes.front: Under 171.1(d)(2), when is unloading hazmat outside the HMR?
notes.back: When the consignee’s employee or contractor unloads after delivery and after the carrier’s personnel, or a private carrier’s driver, have left.
notes.explanation: Unloading is incidental to movement only while carrier personnel are present; once they have gone it is the consignee’s activity.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(2) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: Unloading of a hazardous material from a transport vehicle or a bulk packaging performed by a person employed by or working under contract to the consignee following delivery of the hazardous material by the carrier to its destination and departure from the consignee’s premises of the carrier’s personnel

notes.front: Under 171.1(d)(3), storage of a hazmat package after its delivery by a carrier to the {{c1::destination indicated}} on a shipping document, package marking or other medium is outside the HMR.
notes.explanation: Transportation ends on delivery to that destination, so storage afterwards is no longer incidental to movement.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(3) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: (3) Storage of a freight container, transport vehicle, or package containing a hazardous material after its delivery by a carrier to the destination indicated on a shipping document, package marking, or other medium

notes.front: Under 171.1(d)(4), when are hazmat movements inside a facility still subject to the HMR?
notes.back: When the movement is on or crosses a public road, or is on track that is part of the general railroad system.
notes.explanation: Movements wholly inside a contiguous facility with restricted public access are otherwise given as outside the HMR.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(4) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: Rail and motor vehicle movements of a hazardous material exclusively within a contiguous facility boundary where public access is restricted, except to the extent that the movement is on or crosses a public road or is on track that is part of the general railroad system of transportation

notes.front: Under 171.1(d)(5), which government transport is outside the HMR?
notes.back: Hazmat in a motor vehicle, aircraft or vessel operated by a government employee solely for noncommercial federal, state or local government purposes.
notes.explanation: The word “solely” matters: the example covers only noncommercial government purposes.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(5) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: (5) Transportation of a hazardous material in a motor vehicle, aircraft, or vessel operated by a Federal, state, or local government employee solely for noncommercial Federal, state, or local government purposes.

notes.front: Under 171.1(d)(6), is a person carrying hazmat for non-commercial purposes in a rented car subject to the HMR?
notes.back: No. Transport by an individual for non-commercial purposes in a private motor vehicle, including a leased or rented one, is given as outside the HMR.
notes.explanation: The example expressly includes leased and rented vehicles, so ownership of the car does not matter.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(6) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: (6) Transportation of a hazardous material by an individual for non-commercial purposes in a private motor vehicle, including a leased or rented motor vehicle.

notes.front: Under 171.1(d)(7), any matter subject to the {{c1::postal laws and regulations}} of the United States is outside the HMR.
notes.explanation: The definition of “person” likewise leaves out the United States Postal Service.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(7) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: (7) Any matter subject to the postal laws and regulations of the United States.

notes.front: A chemical distributor keeps pallets of packaged hazmat in its own warehouse for a week, waiting for the carrier it has booked. Is the week in the warehouse subject to the HMR?
notes.back: D: No. Storage at the offeror facility before the carrier takes possession is given as outside the HMR.
notes.explanation: 171.1(d)(1) lists this storage as an example of an activity to which the HMR do not apply.
notes.choices:
A) Only if the warehouse is next to a public road
B) Yes, it is storage incidental to movement
C) Yes, because a carrier has been booked
D) No, storage at the offeror facility before the carrier takes possession is outside the HMR
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: storage incidental to movement starts when a carrier takes physical possession. C is wrong: booking is not taking possession. A is wrong: the public road test belongs to movements inside a facility.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(1) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: Storage of a freight container, transport vehicle, or package containing a hazardous material at an offeror facility prior to a carrier taking possession of the hazardous material for movement in transportation in commerce

notes.front: A tanker driver delivers solvent to a factory and drives away. An hour later, the factory’s own staff pump the remaining solvent out of a delivered tank into storage. How do the HMR treat the pumping?
notes.back: D: As outside the HMR: unloading by the consignee’s staff after the carrier’s personnel have left.
notes.explanation: 171.1(d)(2) gives this unloading, after delivery and after the carrier’s personnel have departed, as an example of an activity outside the HMR.
notes.choices:
A) As unloading incidental to movement
B) As a pre-transportation function
C) As storage incidental to movement
D) As outside the HMR: unloading by the consignee’s staff after the carrier’s personnel have left
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: that needs carrier personnel to perform the unloading or be present. B is wrong: the material is not being prepared for transport. C is wrong: nothing is being stored in transportation; the delivery has ended.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(d)(2) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: performed by a person employed by or working under contract to the consignee following delivery of the hazardous material by the carrier to its destination and departure from the consignee’s premises of the carrier’s personnel

notes.front: Storage before the carrier takes possession, storage in transit, storage after delivery: which of the three is subject to the HMR?
notes.back: Only storage in transit, as storage incidental to movement.
notes.explanation: 171.1(c)(4) places storage between possession and delivery inside transportation; 171.1(d)(1) and (3) give the other two as outside the HMR.
notes.contrast: Before possession (171.1(d)(1)) and after delivery (171.1(d)(3)) are given as outside the HMR.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(c)(4) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 3
notes.evidence: Storage of a transport vehicle, freight container, or package containing a hazardous material by any person between the time that a carrier takes physical possession of the hazardous material for the purpose of transporting it until the package containing the hazardous material has been delivered

notes.front: Under 49 U.S.C. 5125, as 171.1(f) sets out, when is a state requirement preempted because of a clash with federal law?
notes.back: When complying with both the non-federal requirement and the federal hazmat law or regulations is not possible.
notes.explanation: This is the first ground listed; preemption does not apply where another federal statute authorises the rule or a waiver is issued.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(f)(1)(i) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: a requirement of a state, political subdivision of a state, or an Indian tribe is preempted, unless otherwise § 171.1 authorized by another Federal statute or DOT issues a waiver of preemption, if— (i) Complying with both the non-Federal requirement and Federal hazardous materials transportation law

notes.front: Under 171.1(f)(1)(iii), what are two covered subjects on which a non-federal rule must be substantively the same as the federal rule?
notes.back: Any two, among others: designating, describing and classifying hazmat; packing, labelling, marking and placarding; shipping documents.
notes.explanation: On these subjects a state rule that is not substantively the same as the federal one is preempted.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.1(f)(1)(iii) (revised as of 1 October 2025), p. 4
notes.evidence: (A) The designation, description, and classification of hazardous material; (B) The packing, repacking, handling, labeling, marking, and placarding of hazardous material; (C) The preparation, execution, and use of shipping documents related to hazardous material

notes.front: Can a self-employed owner-operator be a hazmat employee?
notes.back: Yes, if they transport hazmat in commerce and, in that self-employment, directly affect hazardous materials transportation safety.
notes.explanation: The definition names owner-operators of motor vehicles, vessels and aircraft.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (ii) Self-employed (including an owner-operator of a motor vehicle, vessel, or aircraft) transporting hazardous materials in commerce who in the course of such self-employment directly affects hazardous materials transportation safety

notes.front: Which two railroad jobs does the hazmat employee definition name outright?
notes.back: A railroad signalman and a railroad maintenance-of-way employee.
notes.explanation: They are listed as hazmat employees in their own right, without the “directly affects safety” test.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (iii) A railroad signalman; or (iv) A railroad maintenance-of-way employee.

notes.front: Under the hazmat employee definition, which activity covers a forklift driver who moves drums of hazmat around a depot?
notes.back: Loading, unloading or handling hazardous materials (171.8, “Hazmat employee” (2)(i)).
notes.explanation: Handling alone is enough; the person need not pack or ship the material.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (2) This term includes an individual, employed on a full time, part time, or temporary basis by a hazmat employer, or who is self-employed, who during the course of employment: (i) Loads, unloads, or handles hazardous materials;

notes.front: Under the hazmat employee definition, which activity covers a technician who tests cylinders sold as qualified for hazmat?
notes.back: Designing, manufacturing, fabricating, inspecting, marking, maintaining, reconditioning, repairing or testing a qualified packaging (item (2)(ii)).
notes.explanation: Packaging work counts even when the person never touches the hazmat itself.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (ii) Designs, manufactures, fabricates, inspects, marks, maintains, reconditions, repairs, or tests a package, container or packaging component that is represented, marked, certified, or sold as qualified for use in transporting hazardous material in commerce.

notes.front: Under the hazmat employee definition, which activity covers a shipping clerk who readies hazmat consignments for collection?
notes.back: Preparing hazardous materials for transportation (item (2)(iii)).
notes.explanation: Preparing a shipment is its own item in the list, separate from handling it.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (iii) Prepares hazardous materials for transportation; (iv) Is responsible for safety of transporting hazardous materials;

notes.front: Under the hazmat employee definition, which activity covers a transport safety manager who never packs or drives?
notes.back: Being responsible for the safety of transporting hazardous materials (item (2)(iv)).
notes.explanation: Responsibility for safety is enough, without doing the physical work.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (iv) Is responsible for safety of transporting hazardous materials; (v) Operates a vehicle used to transport hazardous materials.

notes.front: Under the hazmat employee definition, which activity covers a delivery driver whose van carries hazmat?
notes.back: Operating a vehicle used to transport hazardous materials (item (2)(v)).
notes.explanation: Driving is the last activity in the list.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (v) Operates a vehicle used to transport hazardous materials. Hazmat employer means:

notes.front: Can a self-employed person be a hazmat employer?
notes.back: Yes. A self-employed person, including an owner-operator, who transports hazmat in commerce is a hazmat employer under limb (2).
notes.explanation: The same owner-operator is also named in the hazmat employee definition, so one person can be both.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employer”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (2) A person who is self-employed (including an owner-operator of a motor vehicle, vessel, or aircraft) transporting materials in commerce; and who: (i) Transports hazardous materials in commerce;

notes.front: Can a government body be a hazmat employer?
notes.back: Yes. A federal department or agency, or a state, local or tribal authority, that transports hazmat, causes it to be transported, or makes qualified packagings.
notes.explanation: Limb (3) of the definition covers these public bodies on the same activity tests as private employers.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employer”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (3) A department, agency, or instrumentality of the United States Government, or an authority of a State, political subdivision of a State, or an Indian tribe; and who: (i) Transports hazardous materials in commerce;

notes.front: A lorry driver owns her own tractor unit, works for herself, and hauls tanks of fuel for several shippers. What is she under 171.8?
notes.back: C: Both a hazmat employee and a hazmat employer.
notes.explanation: Both definitions name self-employed owner-operators of a motor vehicle who transport hazmat in commerce.
notes.choices:
A) A hazmat employee only
B) A hazmat employer only
C) Both a hazmat employee and a hazmat employer
D) Neither, because she has no employer
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: limb (2) of the employer definition also covers her. B is wrong: the employee definition names self-employed owner-operators too. D is wrong: self-employment is expressly covered.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee” and “Hazmat employer”, p. 28
notes.evidence: (2) A person who is self-employed (including an owner-operator of a motor vehicle, vessel, or aircraft) transporting materials in commerce; and who: (i) Transports hazardous materials in commerce;

notes.front: A chemical firm takes on a worker on a two-week temporary contract to pack hazmat parcels in its dispatch bay. Is the worker a hazmat employee?
notes.back: B: Yes: temporary staff who directly affect hazmat transport safety are covered.
notes.explanation: The definition covers people employed on a temporary basis by a hazmat employer who directly affect hazardous materials transportation safety.
notes.choices:
A) No, only permanent staff can be hazmat employees
B) Yes: temporary staff who directly affect hazmat transport safety are covered
C) No, because two weeks is too short
D) Only if the worker also drives the vehicle
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the definition names temporary employment. C is wrong: the definition sets no minimum period. D is wrong: driving is only one of the activities; packing for transport also directly affects safety.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazmat employee”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Employed on a full-time, part time, or temporary basis by a hazmat employer and who in the course of such full time, part time or temporary employment directly affects hazardous materials transportation safety

notes.front: Which of these is a carrier under 171.8?
notes.back: C: A ferry company that moves lorries and their loads for payment.
notes.explanation: A carrier transports passengers or property in commerce by rail car, aircraft, motor vehicle or vessel, and a ferry is a vessel.
notes.choices:
A) A laboratory that tests packagings
B) A factory that fills drums and waits for collection
C) A ferry company that moves lorries and their loads for payment
D) A consultant who classifies materials for shippers
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: filling and waiting are pre-transportation activities, not transporting. A is wrong: testing packagings does not move property. D is wrong: classifying is a pre-transportation function.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Carrier”, p. 24
notes.evidence: Carrier means a person who transports passengers or property in commerce by rail car, aircraft, motor vehicle, or vessel.

notes.front: A bulk packaging for a liquid has a maximum capacity greater than {{c1::450 L (119 gallons)}}.
notes.explanation: The same figure is the upper limit for a non-bulk liquid packaging, so the two definitions meet at 450 L.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Bulk packaging”, p. 24
notes.evidence: (1) A maximum capacity greater than 450 L (119 gallons) as a receptacle for a liquid;

notes.front: What makes a packaging for a solid a bulk packaging?
notes.back: A maximum net mass greater than 400 kg (882 pounds) and a maximum capacity greater than 450 L (119 gallons).
notes.explanation: Both tests are joined by “and”, so a solid packaging must pass the mass and the capacity figures.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Bulk packaging”, p. 24
notes.evidence: (2) A maximum net mass greater than 400 kg (882 pounds) and a maximum capacity greater than 450 L (119 gallons) as a receptacle for a solid;

notes.front: A bulk packaging for a gas has a water capacity greater than {{c1::454 kg (1000 pounds)}}.
notes.explanation: For gases the measure is water capacity, not volume or net mass.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Bulk packaging”, p. 24
notes.evidence: (3) A water capacity greater than 454 kg (1000 pounds) as a receptacle for a gas as defined in § 173.115 of this subchapter.

notes.front: Under the non-bulk definition, when is a bag or box non-bulk regardless of the bulk definition?
notes.back: When it has a maximum net mass of 400 kg (882 pounds) or less and conforms to the specification packaging requirements.
notes.explanation: Item (4) opens with “Regardless of the definition of bulk packaging”, so it overrides the capacity tests for these bags and boxes.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Non-bulk packaging”, p. 31
notes.evidence: (4) Regardless of the definition of bulk packaging, a maximum net mass of 400 kg (882 pounds) or less for a bag or a box conforming to the applicable requirements for specification packagings

notes.front: A non-bulk packaging for a solid has a maximum net mass of 400 kg (882 pounds) or less and a maximum capacity of {{c1::450 L (119 gallons)}} or less.
notes.explanation: The same two figures, exceeded together, make a solid packaging bulk.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Non-bulk packaging”, p. 31
notes.evidence: (2) A maximum net mass of 400 kg (882 pounds) or less and a maximum capacity of 450 L (119 gallons) or less as a receptacle for a solid;

notes.front: A shipper fills a 1,000 L tote with a flammable liquid directly, with no inner containers. Which kind of packaging is the tote?
notes.back: D: A bulk packaging.
notes.explanation: A liquid receptacle over 450 L is bulk, and the liquid is loaded with no intermediate form of containment.
notes.choices:
A) A non-bulk packaging, because it is not a tank
B) A freight container
C) A non-bulk packaging, because it can be lifted
D) A bulk packaging
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the test is capacity and containment, not whether it is a tank. B is wrong: a freight container holds packages in unit form. C is wrong: nothing in the liquid test depends on lifting.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Bulk packaging”, p. 24
notes.evidence: (1) A maximum capacity greater than 450 L (119 gallons) as a receptacle for a liquid;

notes.front: A gas receptacle has a water capacity of 300 kg. Which kind of packaging is it?
notes.back: A: A non-bulk packaging.
notes.explanation: For a gas, non-bulk means a water capacity of 454 kg (1000 pounds) or less, and 300 kg is under that.
notes.choices:
A) A non-bulk packaging
B) A bulk packaging, because 300 kg is over 250 kg
C) A freight container
D) A bulk packaging, because every gas receptacle is bulk
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: the definitions set a gas threshold, so not every gas receptacle is bulk. B is wrong: 250 kg is not the threshold; 454 kg is. C is wrong: a freight container is a reusable container of 64 cubic feet or more for packages.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Non-bulk packaging”, p. 31
notes.evidence: (3) A water capacity of 454 kg (1000 pounds) or less as a receptacle for a gas as defined in § 173.115 of this subchapter;

notes.front: Bulk or non-bulk: what figure separates them for a liquid, and on which side does exactly 450 L fall?
notes.back: 450 L (119 gallons); exactly 450 L is non-bulk, because bulk means greater than 450 L.
notes.explanation: The non-bulk definition says “or less” and the bulk definition says “greater than”.
notes.contrast: Bulk: over 450 L liquid, over 454 kg water capacity for a gas, over 400 kg and over 450 L for a solid.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Non-bulk packaging”, p. 31
notes.evidence: A maximum capacity of 450 L (119 gallons) or less as a receptacle for a liquid;

notes.front: Packaging or package: which one includes the contents?
notes.back: The package: a packaging plus its contents. The packaging is the receptacle and the components it needs to contain.
notes.explanation: The two definitions sit side by side in 171.8, and only package mentions contents.
notes.contrast: Packaging: the receptacle and anything needed for its containment function, with or without contents.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Package” and “Packaging”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Package or Outside Package means a packaging plus its contents.

notes.front: A clerk points at a sealed, filled drum of hazmat ready for collection. In HMR terms, what is it?
notes.back: C: A package.
notes.explanation: Once the drum holds its contents it is a packaging plus its contents, which is the definition of a package.
notes.choices:
A) A packaging only
B) A transport vehicle
C) A package
D) A freight container
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the packaging is the drum without regard to contents; filled, it is a package. B is wrong: a transport vehicle carries cargo. D is wrong: a freight container is 64 cubic feet or more and holds packages.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Package”, p. 32
notes.evidence: Package or Outside Package means a packaging plus its contents.

notes.front: A freight train has four rail cars of hazmat behind one locomotive. How many transport vehicles carry hazmat?
notes.back: C: Four.
notes.explanation: Each cargo-carrying body, such as a rail car, is a separate transport vehicle.
notes.choices:
A) Five, counting the locomotive
B) One, the whole train
C) Four
D) None, because trains are not transport vehicles
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: each cargo-carrying body counts on its own. A is wrong: the locomotive is not carrying the hazmat cargo. D is wrong: the definition names rail cars and tank cars.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Transport vehicle”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Each cargo-carrying body (trailer, rail car, etc.) is a separate transport vehicle.

notes.front: The hazardous material definition includes several groups. What are two of them?
notes.back: Any two, among others: hazardous substances; hazardous wastes; marine pollutants; elevated temperature materials.
notes.explanation: The list also takes in materials in the Hazardous Materials Table and those meeting the part 173 hazard class criteria.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous material”, p. 27
notes.evidence: The term includes hazardous substances, hazardous wastes, marine pollutants, elevated temperature materials, materials designated as hazardous in the Hazardous Materials Table (see 49 CFR 172.101), and materials that meet the defining criteria for hazard classes and divisions in part 173

notes.front: A bulk tanker carries a liquid at 110 °C. The liquid is not in the Hazardous Materials Table and meets no hazard class criteria. Is it a hazardous material?
notes.back: C: Yes, as an elevated temperature material, one of the groups the hazmat definition includes.
notes.explanation: A liquid at or above 100 °C in a bulk packaging is an elevated temperature material, and the hazardous material definition takes in that group as well as the table and the class criteria.
notes.choices:
A) No, because it is not in the Hazardous Materials Table
B) No, because it meets no hazard class criteria
C) Yes, as an elevated temperature material, one of the groups the hazmat definition includes
D) Only if it is a hazardous waste
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the table is only one of the groups the definition includes. B is wrong for the same reason: the definition lists other groups too. D is wrong: hazardous waste is a separate group, not a condition.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous material”, p. 27
notes.evidence: The term includes hazardous substances, hazardous wastes, marine pollutants, elevated temperature materials

notes.front: Under the 10-1-25 text, what are the first two conditions a hazardous substance must meet?
notes.back: It is listed in appendix A to 172.101, and one package holds at least its reportable quantity.
notes.explanation: The definition joins its conditions with “and”, so a listed material in a small package does not qualify.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous substance”, p. 27
notes.evidence: (1) Is listed in the appendix A to § 172.101 of this subchapter; (2) Is in a quantity, in one package, which equals or exceeds the reportable quantity (RQ) listed in the appendix A to § 172.101 of this subchapter; and

notes.front: A listed hazardous substance has a reportable quantity of 100 pounds. One package holds 40 pounds of it, unmixed. Under the 10-1-25 text, is that package a hazardous substance?
notes.back: D: No, because the quantity in one package is below the reportable quantity.
notes.explanation: The definition requires a quantity, in one package, that equals or exceeds the reportable quantity.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because every listed material is hazardous in any amount
B) Yes, because the material is listed
C) Yes, if the vehicle carries more than 100 pounds in total
D) No, because the quantity in one package is below the reportable quantity
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: being listed is only one of the conditions. C is wrong: the test is the quantity in one package. A is wrong: the reportable quantity sets a threshold.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous substance”, p. 27
notes.evidence: (2) Is in a quantity, in one package, which equals or exceeds the reportable quantity (RQ) listed in the appendix A to § 172.101 of this subchapter

notes.front: What change to the hazardous substance and reportable quantity definitions takes effect on 2 December 2026?
notes.back: The HMR stop keeping their own list and rely on the list the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency already maintains.
notes.explanation: The final rule describes the HMR’s own list as duplicative and relies instead on the list the Environmental Protection Agency already maintains.
notes.source: PHMSA final rule, 91 FR 49305 (4 August 2026), FR Doc. 2026-15809, summary and dates, p. 1
notes.evidence: this final rule streamlines the Hazardous Materials Regulations by modifying how hazardous substances are listed. Instead of maintaining a duplicative list, the regulations will now rely on the authoritative, comprehensive list already maintained by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. DATES: This final rule is effective December 2, 2026.

notes.front: Hazardous waste or hazardous substance: which one is defined by the Environmental Protection Agency’s manifest requirements?
notes.back: Hazardous waste. A hazardous substance is defined by a listing and a reportable quantity in one package.
notes.explanation: The hazardous waste definition points to the manifest requirements in part 262 of title 40, not to appendix A.
notes.contrast: Hazardous substance: listed in appendix A to 172.101 and at or above its reportable quantity in one package.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous waste”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Hazardous waste, for the purposes of this chapter, means any material that is subject to the Hazardous Waste Manifest Requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency specified in 40 CFR part 262.

notes.front: A workshop’s spent solvent is subject to the Environmental Protection Agency’s hazardous waste manifest rules in part 262 of title 40. What is it under the HMR?
notes.back: A: A hazardous waste, and so a hazardous material.
notes.explanation: The HMR define hazardous waste by that manifest requirement, and hazardous wastes are among the groups the hazardous material definition includes.
notes.choices:
A) A hazardous waste, and so a hazardous material
B) A residue
C) A limited quantity
D) Outside the HMR, because waste is regulated only by the environmental agency
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: the HMR take in hazardous waste through their own definition. B is wrong: a residue is what remains in an emptied packaging. C is wrong: a limited quantity is an amount set in a section for a material.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Hazardous waste”, p. 28
notes.evidence: means any material that is subject to the Hazardous Waste Manifest Requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency specified in 40 CFR part 262.

notes.front: A liquid in a bulk packaging is an elevated temperature material if it is at or above {{c1::100 °C (212 °F)}}.
notes.explanation: This is the first of the three temperature tests in the definition.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Elevated temperature material”, p. 26
notes.evidence: (1) Is in a liquid phase and at a temperature at or above 100 °C (212 °F);

notes.front: When is a heated liquid with a flash point of at least 38 °C (100 °F) an elevated temperature material?
notes.back: When, in a bulk packaging, it is intentionally heated and offered or transported at or above its flash point.
notes.explanation: This second test catches liquids below 100 °C that are heated past their flash point.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Elevated temperature material”, p. 26
notes.evidence: (2) Is in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 38 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point; or

notes.front: A solid in a bulk packaging is an elevated temperature material if it is at or above {{c1::240 °C (464 °F)}}.
notes.explanation: Solids have a much higher threshold than the 100 °C set for liquids.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Elevated temperature material”, p. 26
notes.evidence: (3) Is in a solid phase and at a temperature at or above 240 °C (464 °F).

notes.front: Which gases are materials poisonous by inhalation?
notes.back: Gases meeting the criteria in 173.115(c) and assigned to any of the four hazard zones under 173.116(a).
notes.explanation: Gases can fall in any of four zones; liquids are limited to two.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Material poisonous by inhalation”, p. 31
notes.evidence: (1) A gas meeting the defining criteria in § 173.115(c) of this subchapter and assigned to Hazard Zone A, B, C, or D in accordance with § 173.116(a) of this subchapter;

notes.front: Apart from the gas and liquid criteria, how else can a material be poisonous by inhalation?
notes.back: By being identified as an inhalation hazard by a special provision in column 7 of the 172.101 table.
notes.explanation: The third limb of the definition relies on the table rather than on test criteria.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Material poisonous by inhalation”, p. 31
notes.evidence: (3) Any material identified as an inhalation hazard by a special provision in column 7 of the § 172.101 table.

notes.front: A liquid meets the inhalation toxicity criteria in 173.132(a)(1)(iii) and has been assigned to one of the two liquid hazard zones. It is shipped as a liquid, not a mist. What is it?
notes.back: A: A material poisonous by inhalation (PIH).
notes.explanation: The second limb of the definition covers such liquids, other than as a mist, assigned to a hazard zone under 173.133(a).
notes.choices:
A) A material poisonous by inhalation (PIH)
B) An elevated temperature material
C) A residue
D) Nothing, because only gases can be PIH
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that definition turns on temperature in bulk. C is wrong: a residue is what is left in an emptied packaging. D is wrong: the definition has a limb for liquids.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Material poisonous by inhalation”, p. 31
notes.evidence: (2) A liquid (other than as a mist) meeting the defining criteria in § 173.132(a)(1)(iii) of this subchapter and assigned to Hazard Zone A or B in accordance with § 173.133(a) of this subchapter;

notes.front: Primary hazard or subsidiary hazard: which one is the hazard class assigned in the 172.101 table?
notes.back: The primary hazard. Any other hazard of the material is a subsidiary hazard.
notes.explanation: The subsidiary hazard is defined only by reference to the primary one.
notes.contrast: Subsidiary hazard: a hazard of the material other than the primary hazard (171.8).
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Primary hazard”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Primary hazard means the hazard class of a material as assigned in the § 172.101 table.

notes.front: The 172.101 table assigns a material to a flammable liquid class; the material is also corrosive. What is the corrosivity?
notes.back: A: A subsidiary hazard.
notes.explanation: The class the table assigns is the primary hazard, and any other hazard of the material is a subsidiary hazard.
notes.choices:
A) A subsidiary hazard
B) A second primary hazard
C) Not a hazard for HMR purposes
D) The primary hazard
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: the table assigns flammability as the class. B is wrong: 171.8 says a material is assigned to only one hazard class. C is wrong: the HMR name any other hazard as a subsidiary hazard.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Subsidiary hazard”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Subsidiary hazard means a hazard of a material other than the primary hazard.

notes.front: A tank car has been unloaded as far as practicable but not yet cleaned or purged. What is the chemical left inside it?
notes.back: B: A residue.
notes.explanation: A residue is hazmat remaining after unloading to the maximum extent practicable and before refilling or cleaning and purging.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing regulated, because the car is empty
B) A residue
C) A limited quantity
D) A hazardous waste
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the definition covers what remains after unloading. C is wrong: a limited quantity is an amount set for a material with a packaging or labelling exception. D is wrong: hazardous waste is defined by the manifest requirements, not by being left over.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Residue”, p. 35
notes.evidence: Residue means the hazardous material remaining in a packaging, including a tank car, after its contents have been unloaded to the maximum extent practicable

notes.front: Does every hazardous material have a limited quantity?
notes.back: No. A limited quantity exists only when a section applicable to that particular material specifies one.
notes.explanation: The definition begins “when specified as such in a section applicable to a particular material”.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Limited quantity”, p. 29
notes.evidence: Limited quantity, when specified as such in a section applicable to a particular material

notes.front: A section applicable to a material says small amounts of it are a limited quantity. What does that give a shipper who stays within the amount?
notes.back: A specific labelling or packaging exception for that amount.
notes.explanation: The definition calls the limited quantity the maximum amount for which there is such an exception.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Limited quantity”, p. 29
notes.evidence: means the maximum amount of a hazardous material for which there is a specific labeling or packaging exception.

notes.front: May a trade name be used as a technical name?
notes.back: No, except for names that appear in subpart B of part 172.
notes.explanation: A technical name must be a recognised scientific name or an acceptable generic description.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Technical name”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Except for names which appear in subpart B of part 172 of this subchapter, trade names may not be used as technical names.

notes.front: What are two generic chemical descriptions the HMR give as acceptable technical names?
notes.back: Any two: organic phosphate compounds; petroleum aliphatic hydrocarbons; tertiary amines.
notes.explanation: Generic descriptions are allowed when they readily identify the general chemical group.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Technical name”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Examples of acceptable generic chemical descriptions are organic phosphate compounds, petroleum aliphatic hydrocarbons and tertiary amines.

notes.front: A shipper writes a product’s brand name, which is not in subpart B of part 172, as its technical name. Is that allowed?
notes.back: C: No: trade names may not be used as technical names.
notes.explanation: A technical name is a recognised chemical or microbiological name, or an acceptable generic description, and trade names are excluded.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the brand is well known
B) Yes, if the proper shipping name is also shown
C) No: trade names may not be used as technical names
D) Yes, for domestic shipments only
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the rule has no exception for well-known brands. B is wrong: the proper shipping name does not cure a wrong technical name. D is wrong: the definition makes no domestic exception.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Technical name”, p. 37
notes.evidence: Except for names which appear in subpart B of part 172 of this subchapter, trade names may not be used as technical names.

notes.front: A carrier’s manifest, prepared under subpart C of part 172, travels with a hazmat load. Can it be the shipping paper?
notes.back: Yes. A manifest or other shipping document serving a similar purpose and prepared under subpart C is a shipping paper.
notes.explanation: The definition names shipping orders, bills of lading and manifests, and allows other documents serving the same purpose.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Shipping paper”, p. 35
notes.evidence: Shipping paper means a shipping order, bill of lading, manifest or other shipping document serving a similar purpose and prepared in accordance with subpart C of part 172 of this chapter.

notes.front: In a 172.101 table entry, some words are in Roman type and some in italics. Which words form the proper shipping name?
notes.back: B: Only the words in Roman print.
notes.explanation: The 171.8 definition ties the name to the typeface used in the table, so words in italics are not part of the name.
notes.choices:
A) All of them, in the order shown
B) Only the words in Roman print
C) Only the words in italics
D) Whichever words the shipper chooses
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the definition excludes italics. C is wrong: italics are expressly not the proper shipping name. D is wrong: the name is fixed by the table.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Proper shipping name”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Proper shipping name means the name of the hazardous material shown in Roman print (not italics) in § 172.101 of this subchapter.

notes.front: Proper shipping name or technical name: which one comes from the 172.101 table?
notes.back: The proper shipping name. A technical name is a recognised chemical or microbiological name used in scientific texts.
notes.explanation: One is fixed by the table’s Roman print; the other comes from handbooks, journals and texts.
notes.contrast: Technical name: a recognised chemical or microbiological name, or an acceptable generic description; never a trade name outside subpart B.
notes.source: 49 CFR 171.8 (revised as of 1 October 2025), “Proper shipping name”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Proper shipping name means the name of the hazardous material shown in Roman print (not italics) in § 172.101 of this subchapter.
